idiom_name: Immer produce() structural sharing (fallback: spread copy plus Object.freeze)
implementation_notes: JavaScript has no sharing count and no language-level immutability, so the refcounted handle/body structure is replaced by structural sharing: an update copies only the changed path and reuses every untouched subtree. Immer's produce(base, recipe) is the dominant realization - it applies mutations to a draft proxy, produces a new state and freezes it, which is how React/Redux reducers get copy-on-write without hand-written spreads; the dependency-free form is a spread copy per level ({...state, ...patch}) guarded by Object.freeze. ArrayBuffer and typed arrays are shared by reference, so large binary payloads can be shared as long as they are treated as read-only, with structuredClone (a deep, eager copy) as the escape hatch when a genuinely private copy is required.
pitfalls: An Immer draft must not escape the recipe: keeping a reference and using it later throws, and mutating the base after produce() breaks the whole immutability contract.
Object.freeze is shallow - nested objects stay mutable - and freezing a large graph on every update costs time, so freeze at the boundary rather than per change.
structuredClone is an eager deep copy, the opposite of copy-on-write; calling it on every change reinstates the cost the pattern removes, and it throws DataCloneError for functions or DOM nodes.
Sharing a typed array by reference means a write through one view is visible to every holder; treat shared buffers as read-only or copy explicitly.
